In July 1683, 150,000 Ottoman troops laid siege to Vienna, defended by barely 15,000 starving soldiers. For sixty days, defenders fought a brutal subterranean gunpowder war beneath the walls—until King Jan Sobieski of Poland unleashed 18,000 horsemen in the largest cavalry charge in human history.

5:30 - Wings of Thunder: The Polish Winged Hussars on the Ridge

acts.script: In July 1683, an Ottoman army of one hundred and fifty thousand men surrounded the city of Vienna. Vienna was the golden gate to Central Europe. If it fell, the road to Germany and Italy was wide open. The Austrian Emperor had fled the capital in panic, leaving Count Ernst von Starhemberg with only eleven thousand soldiers and five thousand armed citizens. That meant fifteen thousand starving defenders had to hold off a force ten times their size. Because Vienna's walls were built of solid stone, the Ottoman Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa knew normal cannons wouldn't break them quickly. So he ordered thousands of specialized miners to dig trenches right up to the city moat. Every single tree, house, and church outside the walls was demolished by the defenders to deny the enemy cover. Food ran out in weeks. The citizens were reduced to eating horses, dogs, and rats. Dysentery and fever swept through the barracks, cutting the garrison down to barely four thousand fighting men. Yet Count Starhemberg sent a one-line reply to the Ottoman surrender demand: 'I will fight to the last drop of blood.' Because they couldn't breach the walls from above, the Ottomans began digging underneath them.

acts.script: King Jan Sobieski the Third of Poland had answered the call. He marched thirty thousand Polish troops over three hundred miles to unite with German and Austrian armies at the Danube. At the front rode the most feared heavy cavalry on earth: the Polish Winged Hussars. They wore massive arched wooden wings lined with eagle feathers that made a terrifying whistling roar when galloping at full charge. They carried hollow nineteen-foot lances, designed to out-reach any infantry spear and pierce multiple armored men in a single strike. Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa refused to believe a massive relief army had arrived and kept his best troops attacking the city walls instead of securing the hill. At four in the afternoon on September twelfth, Sobieski's army cleared the dense forests atop the Kahlenberg ridge. At five-thirty, Sobieski ordered the trumpets to sound. Eighteen thousand horsemen gathered in one colossal line. It was the largest cavalry charge in human history. The earth literally shook as the cavalry descended upon the Ottoman camp.

derived_shorts.title: 15,000 Starving Defenders Against 150,000 Ottomans (Vienna 1683)
derived_shorts.hook_sentence: In 1683, fifteen thousand starving defenders were surrounded by an army ten times their size.
derived_shorts.script: In July 1683, an Ottoman army of one hundred and fifty thousand men surrounded Vienna—the golden gate to Central Europe. Because the Emperor fled in panic, Count Ernst von Starhemberg was left with only fifteen thousand men, including armed citizens. Surrounded by a force ten times their size, food ran out in weeks and the garrison was forced to eat horses and rats. When the Grand Vizier demanded unconditional surrender, Starhemberg sent back a single line: 'I will fight to the last drop of blood.' Watch the full video on the channel.

derived_shorts.title: The Gunpowder War Fought 50 Feet Underground (Vienna 1683)
derived_shorts.hook_sentence: Because they couldn't break Vienna's walls from above, the siege moved fifty feet underground.
derived_shorts.script: Because they couldn't break Vienna's stone walls from above, the Ottomans began digging fifty feet underground to plant barrels of gunpowder. To detect the enemy tunnels, defenders placed drums covered in dried peas on cellar floors. Whenever the peas vibrated, Austrian miners dug frantically downward to intercept them. Men fought savage, silent battles in suffocating dirt tunnels with daggers, shovels, and sulfur smoke. On September fourth, a massive mine detonated, blowing a thirty-foot gap in the wall—yet the defenders held the breach with pikes. Watch the full video on the channel.
